extracted.intended_audience: legal scholars, public-administration researchers, and policy analysts studying U.S. federal rulemaking, presidential control, and agency capacity
extracted.subtask_description: Empirical evaluation of factors that affect whether and how quickly federal rulemakings are finalized during a President's first term, using Unified Agenda/Federal Register data and survival analysis. Focuses on agency capacity, structural independence, and presidential control in the United States.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rulemaking inclusion criteria (dataset)
rubrics_metrics.description: A rulemaking enters the dataset if (1) it first appeared in the Unified Agenda during the first term of Bush, Obama, or Trump and (2) the agency published the first NPRM for the rulemaking in the same term.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This exclusion removes rulemakings carried over from prior administrations to better ensure the dataset reflects the current administration's priorities. The author notes verification of Unified Agenda entries with Federal Register publications due to typographical errors and inconsistencies in the Unified Agenda.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude rulemakings carried over from previous administrations
rubrics_metrics.description: Eliminate rules carried over from a previous administration so the dataset is representative of the current administration’s priorities and not prior priorities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: rulemakings begun during the second term of the prior administration are excluded. This helps avoid attributing completion (or non-completion) to the wrong administration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude routine and informational/administrative/other rulemakings
rubrics_metrics.description: Exclude any rulemaking classified as 'routine and frequent' or 'informational/administrative/other' by the agency, because these are unlikely to relate to the President's agenda.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definitions: 'routine and frequent' = recurring applications that do not alter the body of regulation; 'informational/administrative/other' = primarily informational or pertains to agency matters not central to accomplishing the agency’s regulatory mandate. The dataset retains rulemakings classified as 'economically significant', 'other significant', or 'substantive, nonsignificant' (i.e., substantive policy change).

rubrics_metrics.name: Three analytic subsets of rulemakings
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyze rulemakings across three subsets: (a) All Rulemakings begun during the first term; (b) Rulemakings by Executive Agencies (excluding independent commissions); (c) Rulemakings Prioritized by the President (only agencies the President publicly prioritized).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All Rulemakings is the weakest assumption (most data). Executive Agencies subset assumes Presidents better control executive agencies. Prioritized Agencies subset uses measures from Bednar & Lewis (examining first addresses to Congress and campaign documents) and aims to focus on rulemakings more plausibly tied to presidential priorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operationalization of 'prioritized by the President'
rubrics_metrics.description: An agency is treated as prioritized if the President proposed a policy related to the agency's jurisdiction in the President's first address to Congress or in campaign documents (coded using methods from Bednar & Lewis).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This coding assumes that rulemakings begun by priority agencies further the President’s policy objectives and that Presidents make additional efforts to control those agencies’ agendas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dependent variable: rulemaking duration
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure duration as the number of days between the publication of the first NPRM in the Federal Register and the agency's final submission to OIRA (or, if exempt from OIRA review, the final rule's Federal Register appearance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Duration is right-censored at the last day of the President's first term to reflect whether the agency finalized the rule during that term. Censoring addresses rules that remain uncompleted after the first term and helps control for abandoned rulemakings without public notice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary source data and verification
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the Unified Agenda (machine-readable files with RINs) as the standard source for rulemaking data, but verify and correct dates and action types using the Federal Register.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: agencies sometimes strategically manipulate when they report rules to the Unified Agenda; Federal Register publication is a standardized APA requirement and provides an equal point of comparison. The author uses RINs to track rulemakings through time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure of policymaking capacity
rubrics_metrics.description: Policymaking capacity is measured by capacity scores that estimate an agency’s capacity in a given year based on the size, expertise, and experience of the agency's policymaking workforce.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Capacity scores are measured at the start of the administration (or are stable characteristics) to avoid post-treatment bias. The Completion Hypothesis predicts agencies with higher capacity will finalize rulemakings faster and are more likely to complete them before the end of the President’s term.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid post-treatment bias in covariates
rubrics_metrics.description: All independent variables are either (1) stable characteristics that do not change within an administration (e.g., structural characteristics of agency design or stable agency ideology), or (2) measured before the start of the current administration (e.g., policymaking capacity and rulemaking workloads).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This ensures the administration could not have affected these variables, preventing bias from using covariates that change after the 'treatment' (administration began). The paper explicitly avoids including measures like politicization measured after the administration starts to prevent post-treatment bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of survival analysis (Cox proportional hazards model)
rubrics_metrics.description: Estimate time-to-event (rulemaking completion) using a Cox proportional hazard model to handle right-censoring and to estimate both whether higher-capacity agencies complete rules before term end and whether they complete them faster.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: survival models are appropriate for censored duration data; the Cox model has been used in prior rulemaking research. The model controls for confounders and allows interaction tests (e.g., capacity × independence).

rubrics_metrics.name: Control variables for presidential control: structural independence
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure agency structural independence using Selin's coding of statutory features (e.g., removal protections, party-balancing requirements, whether the statute specifies that appointees serve the president).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Independence is treated as exogenous design choices made at agency inception. The paper interacts structural independence with capacity to test the Completion Hypothesis (predicting the marginal effect of independence on duration should decrease as agency capacity decreases).

rubrics_metrics.name: Control variables for presidential control: agency preferences/ideology
rubrics_metrics.description: Include agency preferences (ideological distance) as a covariate related to presidential control; these measures are functions of agency design and are treated as exogenous to current rulemaking activities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agency preferences are included to capture how ideological distance affects presidential influence and rulemaking completion. Measures are selected to avoid being affected by the current administration's rulemaking decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling Unified Agenda strategic disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that agencies sometimes strategically manipulate when they report rules to the Unified Agenda, which may underestimate rulemaking duration if relying solely on the Unified Agenda's first appearance dates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To mitigate this bias, use the date the NPRM first appeared in the Federal Register as a more standardized anchor for duration measurement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection decision about 'economically significant' subset and post-treatment bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Although one could subset to only 'economically significant' or 'other significant' rulemakings, doing so may introduce post-treatment bias because capacity may influence whether an agency decides to pursue a significant change versus an incremental one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Therefore, the author retains the broader set of substantive rulemakings to avoid introducing selection bias that would confound causal inference about capacity.
